profession noun

also professions, by profession, occupation, learned profession

classical

Cic. Off. 1.151
Lewis & Short, s.v. ars: “a profession, art”

ars, artis f.

noun, third declension

a profession, an art (medicine, law, teaching)

The skill one practises and lives by; Cicero sets the arts that call for learning, medicine, architecture and teaching, above the trades of the workshop.

Other words

  • professiō, professiōnis f. — the profession one publicly follows

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 1.21: professiō bene dīcendī (Lewis & Short); Suet. Gramm. (Lewis & Short)

    First a public declaration (of one’s name, property, intentions), then the calling one declares: oratory, the teaching of grammar. Mostly post-Augustan.

Examples

  • quibus autem artibus aut prūdentia major inest aut nōn mediocris ūtilitās quaeritur, ut medicīna, ut architectūra, ut doctrīna rērum honestārum, hae sunt iīs, quōrum ōrdinī conveniunt, honestae

    but the professions that call for more wisdom or bring no small benefit, such as medicine, architecture and the teaching of honourable things, are honourable for those whose station they suitCic. Off. 1.151 (Lewis & Short, s.v. ars)

See also trade, career, professional, job, architecture.
